1.modern-en: Medea is heard wailing inside the house, overwhelmed by Jason's betrayal and his new marriage to Creon's daughter. The Nurse fears her mistress may harm herself, her children, or the royal couple — warning that Medea's fierce spirit will not endure humiliation quietly.

2.modern-en: Medea's voice cries out from within, calling on Zeus, Earth, and the gods of sworn faith to witness Jason's broken vows. The Chorus hears her tormented rage and implores the Nurse to bring her out so they can offer comfort.

3.modern-en: Medea emerges and addresses the Corinthian women directly, outlining the misery of a woman's lot and the particular injustice she faces as a foreigner who sacrificed everything for Jason. When Creon arrives and orders her immediate exile, she grovels strategically to win one extra day — which she intends to use for revenge. In a chilling soliloquy she settles on poison as her weapon against the bride and groom, though she acknowledges she has no plan yet for escape.

4.modern-en: Jason comes to offer help and money for her exile; Medea unleashes a full account of everything she sacrificed for him and rejects his rationalizations. When Aegeus passes through and learns of her plight, she secures a sworn promise of sanctuary in Athens — giving her the escape route she needed to act. She now plots to send the children with poisoned gifts to the bride, and reveals her intention to kill her own sons to inflict the deepest possible wound on Jason.

5.modern-en: Medea summons Jason under a pretense of reconciliation, feigning submission and sending the children to deliver the poisoned robe and golden crown to the princess. She is momentarily undone by tenderness toward her sons but steels herself again, resolving that anger must override love.

6.modern-en: Jason arrives and Medea plays out the deception — weeping convincingly, asking only that the children be allowed to stay in Corinth. The gifts are sent; the Attendant returns with good news that the princess accepted them graciously. Alone, Medea wavers in anguish over killing her children but ultimately resolves to go through with it. She holds them and says farewell.

7.modern-en: The Messenger reports the deaths of the princess and Creon. Medea kills her children inside the house, then escapes on a dragon chariot — beyond Jason's reach. She and Jason trade curses: she will live under Aegeus's protection in Athens; he is left childless, his ship fated to kill him. The Chorus close with the observation that God's ways are beyond all prediction.

epithet.en: Leader of the Argonauts, faithless husband

4.modern-en: Jason arrives claiming goodwill and offering financial help for Medea's exile. He defends his remarriage as a practical political move to secure his family's future, not an act of passion — then leaves when Medea rejects both his money and his reasoning.

6.modern-en: Summoned by Medea's apparent change of heart, Jason comes and is taken in by her performance of repentance. He agrees to plead with the princess on the children's behalf and accepts the poisoned gifts without suspicion, then departs with the children and the Attendant.

7.modern-en: Jason rushes back after hearing of the deaths at the palace, hoping to save his sons — only to be told they are already dead. He beats at the locked doors and then confronts Medea on her dragon chariot, hurling accusations and begging for the bodies. She denies him even that, and he is left desolate, childless, his old ship fated to kill him.

3.modern-en: Creon arrives in person to enforce Medea's immediate exile, citing his fear of her witchcraft and her known threats against his family. He is resolute but yields to Medea's pleading long enough to grant her one more day — a decision he recognizes as foolish even as he makes it.

7.modern-en: Creon does not appear alive. The Messenger reports that he rushed to his dying daughter, embraced her, and was himself destroyed by the clinging poison of the robe — dying alongside her, tangled together in the folds of the garment.

4.modern-en: Aegeus passes through Corinth on his way home from Delphi, where he sought an oracle about his childlessness. When Medea tells him of Jason's betrayal and her exile, he is immediately sympathetic and swears a solemn oath to give her sanctuary in Athens — in exchange for her promise to help him have children. His timely arrival gives Medea the escape route she needs to act.

1.modern-en: The Nurse opens the play alone, recounting the whole backstory of Medea's journey from Colchis and her ruin at Jason's hands. She fears Medea's fierce, unruly spirit and worries she may turn on the children or strike at the royal family — and urges the Attendant to keep the boys away from their mother.

2.modern-en: The Nurse speaks to the arriving Chorus about the dangerous depth of Medea's grief, warning them that her mistress's wrath is like a gathering storm. She reluctantly agrees to try to bring Medea out, knowing words of comfort will likely be useless.

5.modern-en: Medea sends the Nurse to fetch Jason, giving her no hint of her true intentions. The Nurse departs obediently.

1.modern-en: The Attendant brings the children in from play and shares the rumor he overheard: Creon intends to exile Medea and her sons. He and the Nurse agree to keep this from Medea for now, and he takes the children inside, away from their mother's dark mood.

6.modern-en: The Attendant accompanies the children to the palace with the gifts, and returns to Medea with good news — the princess has accepted the gifts warmly and the children's exile has been lifted. He is puzzled by Medea's anguished response to what seems like good news.

7.modern-en: The Messenger arrives in desperate haste to warn Medea to flee, then delivers a horrifying eyewitness account of the princess's death — consumed by the poisoned robe and crown — and of Creon's death as he clung to his dying daughter. He is appalled by Medea's calm pleasure at the news.

1.modern-en: The Chorus of Corinthian women enters as Medea's voice is heard crying inside. They express sympathy for her and concern about the dangerous depths of her grief.

2.modern-en: The Chorus hears Medea's outpourings of rage and grief and urges the Nurse to bring her out. They lament the weight of sorrow that falls on abandoned wives and the strange silence of male poets on women's suffering.

3.modern-en: After Creon leaves, the Chorus expresses anxiety for Medea's future and where she will go. The Leader agrees to keep Medea's revenge plans secret, and the women note that anger between former lovers is the most terrible thing in the world.

4.modern-en: The Chorus reflects on the reversal of old stories — woman shall now be feared, not mocked — and on the cost of exile and homelessness. They warmly welcome Aegeus's departure and praise his kindness.

5.modern-en: The Chorus sings of Athens's beauty and then turns to challenge Medea directly, warning her that she cannot kill her own children and begging her to stop, even kneeling in supplication.

6.modern-en: The Leader weeps as Medea sends her sons off with the poisoned gifts, and the women sing a lament anticipating the princess's death. They also reflect on the sorrow of parenthood. When Medea wavers between love and murderous resolve, they witness her final decision in horror.

7.modern-en: The Chorus calls on the Sun and Earth to stop Medea before she kills her children, then falls silent as the cries of the boys are heard within. At the end, they observe that what happened was beyond all human expectation — the paths God opens are never the ones people foresee.

1.modern-en: Glauce is not present but is the cause of the crisis: Jason has married her to secure his political position in Corinth, abandoning Medea. The Nurse describes her as the new "head and chief" of Jason's household.

6.modern-en: Glauce receives Medea's children and their poisoned gifts — the embroidered robe and golden crown — with delight. The Attendant reports that she accepted them warmly and Jason has won her over to allow the children to stay.

7.modern-en: The Messenger gives a detailed account of Glauce's death: she dressed herself happily in the gifts, then was consumed by magical fire that melted the crown into her flesh and caused the robe to burn her alive. Her father Creon died trying to embrace her.
